title: Precision and Recall for Time Series
problem_setting: The paper addresses evaluation metrics for time series anomaly detection algorithms, proposing a range-based generalization of classical precision/recall to score predicted anomaly ranges against ground-truth (pre-labeled) real anomaly ranges in univariate numeric time series. It is a metric/evaluation-methodology paper, not an online detection or adaptation system.
how_normal_data_selected: n/a: this is an evaluation-metric paper; datasets used come with pre-existing, already-known ground-truth anomaly ranges (e.g., from NAB Data Corpus or the Paranom synthetic generator), and the metric is applied post hoc to detector outputs, not used to select 'normal' training data online.
datasets_and_protocol: Real datasets from the NAB Data Corpus (NYC-Taxi, Twitter-AAPL, Machine-Temp) plus synthetic/augmented datasets generated with the Paranom tool (ECG, Space-Shuttle, Sine, Time-Guided). Protocol: compute range-based RecallT, PrecisionT, and F1-Score (via harmonic mean) under various positional-bias (δ) and cardinality (γ) settings, and compare against classical point-based precision/recall and the Numenta (NAB) scoring model across the three Numenta application profiles (Standard, Reward-Low-FP, Reward-Low-FN); also report a computational cost analysis (naive vs. optimized complexity) for the new metrics.
actual_contribution: The paper introduces a new mathematical model that extends classical precision and recall to range-based anomalies, incorporating existence, size, position, and cardinality of overlaps between predicted and real anomaly ranges, with tunable bias functions (α, γ, ω, δ). It demonstrates that this model provably subsumes classical point-based precision/recall under specific parameter settings, shows through experiments on multiple real/synthetic datasets and three anomaly detectors (LSTM-AD, Greenhouse, Luminol) that it captures distinctions (e.g., positional bias, fragmentation) missed by the classical model and by the Numenta (NAB) scoring model, and provides an optimized algorithm reducing computation from O(Nr×Np) to O(max{Nr,Np}).

title: MemStream: Memory-Based Streaming Anomaly Detection
problem_setting: Unsupervised anomaly detection in multi-dimensional (multi-aspect) data streams arriving over time, where concept drift is present; the model receives no labels and must score each incoming record as anomalous or normal in an online fashion.
how_normal_data_selected: A feature extractor and memory are initially trained/initialized on a small subset of data D assumed normal; thereafter, an incoming record is added to memory only if its discounted anomaly score falls below a user-defined threshold beta.
how_anomaly_contamination_prevented: yes: the update threshold beta gates memory updates so that records with a discounted KNN-based anomaly score above beta do not enter memory ('This step ensures that anomalous records do not enter the memory'); additionally, a discounting K-nearest-neighbour scoring scheme (gamma) provides a self-correction/recovery mechanism if an anomalous element does enter memory.
drift_vs_anomaly_explicitly_distinguishe: yes: mechanism is memory size relative to distributional spread and drift speed (Proposition 1) plus the FIFO update policy and threshold beta, which is framed as capturing 'how frequently the memory should be updated, or how close is the stream to the initial data distribution' to avoid flagging gradual drift as anomalous while still catching genuine anomalies.
rollback_or_reset: yes: periodic retraining ('quick retraining when the arriving stream becomes sufficiently different from the training data') and a self-correction/recovery mechanism via K-nearest-neighbour discounting (gamma) that lets the algorithm recover if the memory becomes poisoned with anomalous elements.
uses_model_internal_state_as_evidence: yes: the memory module's stored encodings (K-nearest-neighbour distances to items currently in memory) are used directly as the anomaly score for each incoming record.
model_specific_or_agnostic: specific: denoising autoencoder (or PCA/Information Bottleneck) feature extractor plus an explicit FIFO memory module with KNN-based scoring
requires_retraining: yes: the feature extractor (denoising autoencoder) can be periodically fine-tuned/retrained at intervals across the stream when the stream drifts sufficiently far from the original training data
datasets_and_protocol: KDDCUP99, NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, CICIDS-DoS, and 7 ODDS datasets (Ionosphere, Cardio, Satellite, Satimage-2, Mammography, Pima, ForestCover), plus 2 synthetic datasets (Syn and a drift-scenario synthetic set); evaluated primarily via ROC-AUC (and AUC-PR plus runtime for NSL-KDD), compared against 11 streaming baselines (STORM, HS-Tree, iForestASD, RS-Hash, RCF, LODA, Kitsune, DILOF, xStream, MStream, Extended Isolation Forest), each run 5 times with mean reported.
actual_contribution: The paper presents MemStream, a streaming anomaly detection framework combining a denoising autoencoder feature extractor with an explicit FIFO memory module scored via discounted K-nearest-neighbour distance, and proves a theoretical bound on memory size needed to handle concept drift as well as an architecture-design proposition motivating output dimension choice. It demonstrates empirically that MemStream outperforms 11 state-of-the-art streaming baselines in AUC/AUC-PR across 2 synthetic and 11 real-world datasets, adapts quickly to several concept-drift scenarios, benefits from periodic retraining on long drifting streams, and can self-correct/recover from a memory-poisoning event via its discounting mechanism.

title: Towards a Rigorous Evaluation of Time-series Anomaly Detection
venue: AAAI 2022 (per M2N2 reference list: AAAI v36i7)
problem_setting: Unsupervised multivariate time-series anomaly detection (TAD) where models are trained on normal-only data and evaluated on a labeled test set; the paper critiques the point adjustment (PA) evaluation protocol and existing benchmark comparisons rather than proposing a new detector.
how_normal_data_selected: n/a: standard unsupervised TAD setup where training data is assumed normal by dataset construction (e.g., first days of SWaT/WADI/SMD collection contain only normal operation); paper does not propose a selection mechanism, only analyzes existing benchmark train/test splits
datasets_and_protocol: SWaT, WADI, SMD, MSL, SMAP. Evaluates using F1 score with and without point adjustment (F1PA vs F1), Pearson/Kendall correlation between F1PA and F1, and proposes a new PA%K protocol (F1 computed with partial point adjustment applied only if the fraction of detected points in a segment exceeds threshold K, with AUC over K in [0,100]) plus comparison against baselines (random anomaly score, input norm as anomaly score, untrained randomly-initialized encoder-decoder).
actual_contribution: The paper shows theoretically and experimentally that the point adjustment (PA) protocol can make even random or untrained anomaly scores achieve F1PA comparable to state-of-the-art TAD methods, making PA-based rankings unreliable. It further shows that without PA, many existing TAD methods do not significantly outperform simple untrained baselines (random score, input norm, randomly initialized encoder-decoder). Based on these findings it proposes using an untrained-model baseline for comparison and a new PA%K evaluation protocol that interpolates between F1 and F1PA to mitigate both overestimation and underestimation of detection performance.

problem_setting: Multi-horizon time-series forecasting (predicting future covariate values from observed inputs) on non-stationary multivariate time-series data from domains like healthcare, finance, retail, and energy, using supervised learning with encoder-decoder deep neural networks (LSTM Seq2Seq and TFT).

title: Efficient Test-Time Model Adaptation without Forgetting
problem_setting: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for image classification, where a trained deep model must adapt online to distribution-shifted (corrupted/rendition) test images using only unlabeled test samples, with no access to source training data or labels.
how_normal_data_selected: n/a: the paper's analogue to 'normal' data is a small set of unlabeled in-distribution (ID) test samples, collected via existing out-of-distribution detection techniques (Liu et al., 2020; Berger et al., 2021), then pseudo-labeled by the frozen base model to compute Fisher importance.
how_anomaly_contamination_prevented: yes: an entropy-based reliability score excludes high-entropy (unreliable) samples from contributing gradients during adaptation (Eqn. 3), combined with a diversity-based score that filters out redundant samples with similar predictions (Eqn. 5); together these form the active sample weight S(x) used to gate backward updates.
rollback_or_reset: yes: in the non-lifelong evaluation protocol, model parameters are reset to the original trained weights before adaptation begins on each new corruption/test set; episodic variants (TTT/Tent episodic) reset parameters after every single optimization step; a 'lifelong' variant with no resets is also evaluated for comparison.
uses_model_internal_state_as_evidence: yes: (1) the entropy of the model's softmax output E(x;Θ) is used per-sample to decide reliability/inclusion in adaptation; (2) the diagonal Fisher information matrix (computed from pseudo-labeled ID samples) is used as a per-parameter importance weight for an anti-forgetting regularizer constraining BN affine parameters.
model_specific_or_agnostic: specific: convolutional networks with batch normalization layers (ResNet-26/50/101/152); only BN affine parameters are updated at test time.
datasets_and_protocol: CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C (15 corruption types x 5 severity levels), and ImageNet-R. Evaluation via classification/corruption error (%) on OOD test sets, clean accuracy (%) on original in-distribution validation data (measuring forgetting), and efficiency measured by number of forward and backward passes; compared against TTT, TTA, BN adaptation, MEMO, and Tent under both 'reset-per-dataset' and 'lifelong' (never reset) adaptation protocols.
actual_contribution: The paper proposes EATA, which combines (1) an active/sample-adaptive entropy minimization scheme that filters out high-entropy and redundant test samples to reduce unnecessary backward passes, and (2) a Fisher-information-based regularizer computed from pseudo-labeled ID test samples to prevent important parameters from drifting during test-time adaptation. It demonstrates on CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R that this reduces the number of backward computations relative to Tent/TTT/MEMO while improving OOD accuracy, and that it substantially mitigates catastrophic forgetting of in-distribution (clean) accuracy compared to Tent, including under long-horizon 'lifelong' adaptation without parameter resets.

problem_setting: Test-time adaptation (TTA) of an image classifier (ResNet-50, ViT-B-16) to a long, non-stationary sequence of test domains (corruption/style shifts) using only unlabeled test batches, with no access to source training data or true target labels.
